sections.heading: Scaling laws: the straight line that moved a trillion dollars
bullets: The empirical discovery behind the whole buildout: a model's error falls smoothly and predictably as compute, data, and parameters increase — plotted on log-log axes (both scales in powers of ten), the relationship is a straight line spanning many orders of magnitude

That straight line is a power law: each doubling of input buys a consistent fractional improvement — diminishing returns, but predictable diminishing returns, and the predictability is the part that changed everything

Predictability de-risks capital: if you can forecast what a ten-times-larger training run will achieve before spending on it, a nine-figure run becomes an engineering decision rather than a gamble — scaling laws are why investors funded compute before products existed

The laws also prescribe balance: compute, data, and model size must grow together, since starving one wastes the others — and when an ingredient plateaus, like high-quality text, the frontier shifts to new scaling axes such as letting models think longer per answer

sections.heading: Training vs inference: the one-time cost and the forever cost
bullets: Training is a one-time expense like building a factory: months of thousands of chips producing a file of model weights; inference — actually answering queries — is the forever cost, paid per use, for every user, for the model's entire service life

The two costs scale on different axes: training cost is set by ambition (how large a run you choose to attempt); inference cost is set by success (how many people use the result) — a popular model's lifetime inference bill can dwarf its training run

Per-query costs fall relentlessly through optimization — smaller distilled models, lower-precision arithmetic, better serving software — while usage grows faster still; the race between falling unit cost and rising volume is what decides the margin

Utilization ties the halves together: training clusters run flat-out by design, but inference fleets must be sized for peak demand and sit partly idle off-peak — and an idle accelerator burns depreciation without earning, making load-smoothing an economics problem

sections.heading: The compute offtake: project finance comes to AI
bullets: The pattern is imported from the power industry: just as a plant gets financed when a creditworthy buyer signs decades of purchase commitments, an AI lab's multi-year, gigawatt-denominated compute commitment is the document a data-center builder borrows against

The chain of dependency follows: lenders finance the builder against the lab's promised payments, so the structure's credit quality reduces to one question — can a fast-growing but unprofitable private company actually pay for a decade? Everyone in the chain is underwriting that single bet

Commitments outrunning revenue is the design, not an accident: a lab can announce hundreds of billions in compute obligations against single-digit billions of revenue, bridged by serial equity raises — the structure holds exactly as long as capital markets believe the growth curve

Contract terms carry the real risk allocation: duration, termination rights, and delivery milestones decide who eats the loss if demand or technology shifts — a decade-long commitment with narrow exits is simultaneously the strongest collateral and the deepest obligation

sections.heading: The model-lab business model
bullets: A frontier lab sells intelligence three ways: metered API access (developers pay per token — the word-fragments text is chopped into), consumer subscriptions (flat monthly price for an assistant), and enterprise agreements adding security, admin controls, and custom terms

Each line has different economics: API revenue scales with other people's products but competes on price per token; subscriptions decouple revenue from usage so light users subsidize heavy ones; enterprise adds sales cost but brings larger, stickier contracts

The free tier is strategy, not charity: hundreds of millions of unpaid users form a conversion funnel, a default-status moat, and a feedback source — while presenting rivals with an inference bill they must match just to compete for the same position

The unresolved question is durability: capability leads decay as rivals catch up within months, so labs race to convert temporary model advantages into durable assets — brand default status, developer ecosystems, enterprise integrations — before the frontier commoditizes

sections.heading: Post-training: teaching the predictor to behave
bullets: Pretraining produces a next-word predictor — a system that continues any text plausibly but has no built-in notion of being helpful, honest, or safe; post-training is the second phase that shapes raw prediction into an assistant

Instruction tuning comes first: fine-tuning on curated examples of questions paired with good answers teaches the format of following directions — the model learns what kind of continuation is actually wanted

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) refines it: humans rank alternative answers, a separate reward model learns to predict those preferences, and the main model is trained to score well against it — optimizing toward judgments too subtle to write down as rules

The newest axis is reasoning training: rewarding models for multi-step work that reaches verifiably correct answers in math and code — teaching them to spend more computation thinking per question, which shifts cost from bigger training runs toward longer answers

sections.heading: Compute as the governed resource
bullets: Inside a lab, compute is allocated like a wartime resource: research experiments, flagship training runs, and revenue-serving inference all compete for the same accelerators — the allocation spreadsheet is the strategy, made physical

Compute is also the lever regulators reach for: capability roughly tracks training compute, so oversight frameworks set thresholds — total operations used in training — above which extra reporting or evaluation applies; imperfect, but observable and countable

Concentration is the governance dilemma: frontier-scale training is affordable to only a handful of organizations, which places societally consequential decisions inside a few private compute budgets — the reason 'who gets compute' became a policy question

Labs experiment with unusual corporate structures — nonprofit oversight, capped returns, public-benefit charters — attempts to hard-wire mission into governance; whether those structures survive trillion-dollar capital needs is one of the era's live experiments

flashcards.q: What is a scaling law in AI?
flashcards.a: An empirical regularity: model error falls smoothly as compute, data, and parameters grow, forming a straight line on log-log axes across many orders of magnitude. Each doubling of input buys a consistent fractional improvement — diminishing returns, but predictable ones.

flashcards.q: Why did scaling laws unlock billions in AI investment?
flashcards.a: Predictability converts gambling into engineering: if you can forecast what a 10x-larger training run will achieve before paying for it, a nine-figure budget becomes a calculated decision. Investors funded compute ahead of products because the capability-per-dollar curve was already visible.

flashcards.q: Why must compute, data, and model size grow together?
flashcards.a: Starving one ingredient wastes the others — a giant model trained on too little data underperforms a smaller model trained in balance. And when one ingredient plateaus, like high-quality text, the frontier shifts to new scaling axes such as spending more computation per answer at inference time.

flashcards.q: How do training and inference costs scale differently?
flashcards.a: Training is a one-time factory-build: its cost is set by how ambitious a run you choose. Inference is the forever cost, paid per query for the model's whole life — set by how successful the product becomes. A popular model's lifetime inference bill can dwarf its training run.

flashcards.q: Why is utilization the hidden variable in inference economics?
flashcards.a: Inference fleets must be sized for peak demand, so they sit partly idle off-peak — and an idle accelerator burns depreciation without earning anything. Smoothing load across time zones, batching queries, and routing to smaller models are economics tools as much as engineering ones.

flashcards.q: How does a compute commitment finance someone else's data center?
flashcards.a: Exactly like a power purchase agreement finances a power plant: the lab's multi-year promise to pay for capacity is bankable revenue, and lenders finance the builder against it. The whole chain's credit quality reduces to whether the lab can pay for a decade.

flashcards.q: How can a lab commit hundreds of billions against single-digit-billion revenue?
flashcards.a: The bridge is serial equity raises against a steep growth curve — commitments are sized to projected, not current, revenue. The structure holds as long as capital markets keep believing the curve; the moment they don't, the same commitments become the overhang.

flashcards.q: What are the three revenue lines of a model lab, and how do their economics differ?
flashcards.a: Metered API (pay per token — scales with others' products, price-competitive), consumer subscriptions (flat fee decouples revenue from usage; light users subsidize heavy ones), and enterprise agreements (higher sales cost, larger and stickier contracts). Most labs run all three at different margins.

flashcards.q: What does a massive free tier buy an AI lab?
flashcards.a: A conversion funnel, default-status habit formation, and usage feedback — plus a strategic tax on competitors, who must match a giant unpaid inference bill just to contest the same position. It's expensive distribution, purchased with compute instead of advertising.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between pretraining and post-training?
flashcards.a: Pretraining produces a raw next-word predictor from huge text corpora — fluent but with no notion of helpfulness or safety. Post-training shapes it into an assistant: instruction tuning teaches the format of following directions, then preference-based methods refine judgment.

Humans rank alternative model answers; a separate reward model learns to predict those rankings; then the main model is optimized to score highly against the reward model. It encodes judgments too subtle to write as rules — the technique that turned raw predictors into usable assistants.

flashcards.q: Why do regulators use training compute as an oversight threshold?
flashcards.a: Capability roughly tracks the total operations used in training, and compute — unlike 'intelligence' — is observable, countable, and hard to hide at frontier scale. Thresholds trigger reporting or evaluation duties above a set size. It's an imperfect proxy, but it's the measurable one.
